title: A guide to Gregorian chant
introduction: The following lessons set forth the elements of Gregorian notation, rhythm, and psalmody, according to the practical teaching of the 1961 Liber Usualis.

blocks.title: The notes and the melody
blocks.text:
In Gregorian chant the words are clothed in a single melodic line. The signs called neumes represent one or more notes sung upon a syllable; their position indicates the ascent or descent of the melody. No previous knowledge of modern notation is required. The notes are read from left to right, except that in the podatus the lower of the two superposed notes is sung first.

The present guide follows the practical Solesmes interpretation given in the 1961 Liber Usualis, with explanations adapted for Hours. The instrumental examples serve to illustrate pitch and rhythm; they cannot render the pronunciation of the Latin or all the delicate inflections of the voice.

blocks.title: The staff and the clefs
blocks.text:
The staff consists of four lines, counted from below upwards: the first is the lowest, and the fourth the highest. The three intervening spaces are likewise counted upwards. Notes are placed upon the lines or in the spaces; passage to the next line or space represents one degree of the scale. A short ledger line supplies a place for notes beyond the staff. In the source notation, no more than one is used above or below.

The clef, written at the beginning of the staff, gives the name and place of the notes. The C clef marks Do, and the F clef marks Fa. The Liber Usualis describes their shapes as ancient forms of the letters C and F. The names Do and Ti are used here for the source’s Doh and Te.

blocks.title: Recognizing the C clef
blocks.text:
The C clef is the sign with two portions surrounding a central opening. The line passing through this opening is the line of Do. The sign itself is not a note to be sung; it gives the point from which the notes are read. A note centred upon that line is Do, the space immediately above is Re, and the space immediately below is Ti.

From Do, count upwards through Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti, Do; downwards, count Ti, La, Sol, Fa, Mi, Re, Do. Each successive line or space advances one degree. These degrees are not all equal intervals: Mi–Fa and Ti–Do are semitones, while the other adjacent degrees are a whole tone apart.

blocks.title: Do on the second, third, or fourth line
blocks.text:
The Liber Usualis places the C clef sometimes on the second line, often on the third, and very often on the fourth. In each position the meaning is the same: its line is Do. Thus, with the clef on the third line, a note on that line is Do; with the clef on the fourth line, a note on the third line is La, and Do lies one line above it. The name of a note cannot be determined from its height on the staff until the clef has been read.

The opening comparison names every line and intervening space, proceeding from the bottom upwards. Select each clef position and observe where Do falls. With the second-line clef the first note is La; with the third-line clef it is Fa; with the fourth-line clef it is Re. The notes occupy the same written places in all three versions, but their names and sounding pitches change with the clef.

blocks.title: Why the position of the clef changes
blocks.text:
The source explains that the clef is shifted to enable melodies of different ranges to be written upon the staff. Placing Do lower leaves more room above it; placing Do higher leaves more room below it. This concerns the convenient writing of the melody. It does not prescribe an absolute singing pitch, nor does the C clef signify that the piece is in the mode of Do.

When the clef and all the notes are moved together by the same number of staff positions, the melody retains its intervals and may be sung at the same pitch. The comparison above gives Do–Re–Mi–Re–Do under several clefs. Unlike the opening comparison, the notes themselves move with the clef, and the sound remains the same.

The F clef applies the same principle to Fa. The Liber Usualis places it as a rule on the third line and rarely on the fourth. From the line of Fa, the space below is Mi, the next line below is Re, and the next space is Do. Both F-clef positions are included in the comparison.

blocks.title: The guide, or custos
blocks.text:
At the end of a staff the custos indicates beforehand the first note of the following staff. It is a guide to the singer and has no sound of its own. It may also precede a change of clef within the same line, showing the pitch of the note which follows. The written position then changes, while the pitch is retained.

If the clef changes within a melody, read the guide according to the old clef, then find that same pitch under the new clef. The source expressly distinguishes this change of written position from a change of pitch. Thereafter, read each note according to the new clef.

blocks.title: The flat and the natural
blocks.text: The flat lowers Ti by a semitone. Within the melody its effect continues for the remainder of the word, unless a division or a natural intervenes. A new word, any division, even a quarter bar, or a natural restores the unaltered note. When placed beside the clef, the flat applies throughout the piece, except where a natural temporarily cancels it. These signs alter pitch only; they add no note to the melody.

blocks.title: The choice of pitch and the modes
blocks.text:
Plainsong notation indicates the relative pitch of the intervals, without prescribing an absolute pitch. The melody is therefore to be taken at a pitch suited to the compass of the singers, its intervals remaining unaltered. This transposition may be heard by means of the Schola pitch and Register controls in the Cantor Guide.

A change of mode is more than a change of pitch. The note of repose, the characteristic intervals, the compass, and the course of the melody give each mode its character. The Roman numeral at the beginning of a piece refers to the traditional eight modes, although this classification does not express the whole variety of Plainsong. A melody employing the notes of the scale of Do need not have Do for its tonic.

blocks.title: The divisions of the melody
blocks.text: The divisions of Plainsong do not imply the regularly recurring strong beats of modern measured music. They distinguish the parts of the phrase and indicate its breathing; a note receives no accent merely because it follows a bar. In the Solesmes account, groups of two and three are freely interwoven within the larger musical sentence. Their relation is considered in the lessons on rhythm.

blocks.title: The form and value of neumes
blocks.text:
A neume unites its notes in a single melodic movement. Each pitch is to be distinctly sounded, without sliding from one to another. Ordinary notes have the same elementary value, whether square, tailed, or diamond-shaped. The tail does not of itself require an accent, nor does the diamond diminish the duration. Dots and other rhythmic signs have their own significance, explained separately.

The simpler groups should first become familiar to the eye and ear. The names of compound neumes may then be consulted as occasion requires. As the source observes, recognition of their constituent groups is of greater practical use than the mere learning of such names as flexus and resupinus.

blocks.title: Duration, rhythm, and intensity
blocks.text:
In the practical rules of the source, a mora dot gives the preceding note twice its ordinary value. The horizontal episema indicates a gentle broadening, whose amount is not fixed. When it extends over several notes, their unity must be preserved; the more frequently such broadening occurs, the more discreetly it should be made.

The vertical episema marks the rhythmic step, or ictus. Ordinarily it neither lengthens the note nor requires an accent. Both episemata may occur upon the same note; the special case of the salicus is explained below. The degree of intensity belongs to the words and to the course of the phrase, and cannot be determined by a rhythmic sign alone.

blocks.title: The integrity of the word
blocks.text:
The neume and its syllable form part of a word, whose unity must be preserved. Care must therefore be taken neither to breathe immediately before a new syllable of the same word, nor to prolong indiscriminately the ending of every group. The text should first be read as a whole, that its meaning may govern the musical phrase.

At the close of a phrase the voice should diminish gently. The pause is proportioned to the importance of the division and to the movement of the chant. Where two long notes conclude the phrase, the last continues this relaxation and receives no fresh impulse.

blocks.title: The taking of breath
blocks.text:
The comma permits a brief breath, taken from the value of the preceding note without disturbing the movement. In an elaborate melody, breathing may be necessary between the printed divisions. A lesser melodic division should then be chosen, preferably at a long note, and the rhythm preserved. If a melisma exceeds the singer’s breath, a discreet breath during the vowel is preferable to a break immediately before the following syllable.

The instrumental examples illustrate the divisions of the phrase; they do not reproduce the act of breathing or its precise duration. In the source’s example of the half bar, the preceding dotted note is shortened to allow for the breath.

blocks.title: The rise and fall of rhythm
blocks.text:
In the Solesmes method, rhythm comprises a rising movement and a coming to rest, termed arsis and thesis. Within the larger movement occur lesser rhythmic steps, as the steps of one ascending or descending a hill. Thus a rhythmic fall may belong to an ascending phrase, and a rhythmic rise to a descending phrase.

The ictus marks this rhythmic step or point of alighting. It is distinct from intensity, from the accent of the word, and from the strong beat of modern measured music. Its influence may be felt in the balance of the voice without an audible stress. The Latin accent is light and lifted; it may fall upon the ictus or between successive ictus points.

blocks.title: The placing of the ictus
blocks.text:
The rules are to be applied in their proper order. First come notes marked with a vertical episema. Next come sustained notes and combinations: dotted notes, bivirga, distropha, tristropha, pressus, oriscus, and the note preceding a quilisma. Lastly, the first note of a group receives the ictus, provided that neither of the preceding rules is thereby contradicted.

Thus the pressus may displace the ictus from the beginning of a written neume, while the special marking of the salicus takes precedence over the group’s first note. A horizontal episema commonly accompanies the ictus, though not invariably; the source gives “corda” in the Alleluia Veni Sancte as an exception. Two rhythmic steps of single value cannot immediately succeed one another; sustained notes admit a different treatment.

blocks.title: Passages without rhythmic signs
blocks.text:
Where more than three ordinary notes occur between successive ictus points, a subdivision is required. Four notes give 2 + 2; five may give either 2 + 3 or 3 + 2. For unmarked syllabic passages, the source proposes two methods: counting backwards by twos from the last certain ictus, or following the melody and words, with preference for word endings and suitable accents, and avoiding weak penultimate syllables where possible.

These principles may admit more than one application. The source acknowledges such differences and counsels agreement among the singers for the sake of unity. The indications and examples in this guide are to be understood in that spirit; they do not prescribe a mechanical succession of accents.

blocks.title: The larger musical phrase
blocks.text: The groups of two and three are subordinate to the larger musical sentence. Its principal divisions are made known by the notation and the punctuation of the text. An ascent should acquire life, and a descent pass gently towards repose, without exaggerated contrast. An elaborate melisma may possess a musical order of its own, governed by these same principles of movement and rest. The instrumental examples assist in following this order; its union with the meaning of the words belongs to the singer.

blocks.title: The parts of the psalm tone
blocks.text:
The psalm tone comprises an intonation, a tenor or reciting note, a mediation at the middle asterisk, and a final cadence. A long first half may be subdivided by a flex, marked with a cross, at which the melody descends. The final cadence joins the psalm suitably to its antiphon.

In ordinary psalmody the intonation is used for the first verse; the succeeding verses begin upon the tenor. It is repeated where the book so directs, as in the Magnificat. If several psalms, or divisions concluded separately, are sung under one antiphon, the cantor intones the first verse of each as far as the mediation. An intonation of two or three groups is assigned respectively to the first two or three syllables.

blocks.title: The syllables of the cadence
blocks.text:
Cadences are of one or two accents, with one, two, or three preparatory syllables. In the Liber Usualis the accents are printed in heavy type and the preparatory syllables in italics. The preparation is found by counting backwards from the cadence accents; the same number of syllables cannot be assigned indiscriminately to every ending.

In certain formulas a word accented on the third-last syllable requires an additional note. This is represented by a hollow note in the general formula, its pitch being shown in the first worked verse. The hollow note thus indicates a possible addition, to be employed only when the syllables require it.

blocks.title: The solemn formulas and Tonus Peregrinus
blocks.text:
The more elaborate formulas used with the Magnificat require the same attention to preparation and accent. For a solemn cadence of modes I and VI, the Liber Usualis permits the reckoning of one accent with three preparatory syllables, while also recording the Vatican description of two accents. This qualification belongs to the teaching of the source and is not to be extended without distinction to other editions.

In the Tonus Peregrinus the reciting note changes. The source also permits G to be added before B-flat at the mediation, giving an optional formula of one accent with three preparatory syllables. Exceptions to the usual descending departure from the tenor include the solemn fifth-mode mediation and the Holy Saturday Compline Tonus in directum. In each case the formula supplied with the psalm is to be consulted.

blocks.title: 8G: the eighth tone, ending G
blocks.text:
In the verse above the C clef stands on the highest line of the four-line staff. That line is Do; below it lie Ti in the space, La on the next line, Sol in the next space, and Fa on the next line. The space immediately above Do is Re. These names express the written relationships, whatever pitch is chosen for singing.

The intonation gives Di = Sol and xit = La; Dó-mi-nus then reaches the tenor Do. Recitation continues on Do through Dó-mi-no. At the mediation, mé rises to Re and o returns to Do. The asterisk divides the verse, and the second half resumes upon Do.

At the ending, Sé-de a remains on Do. Count back from the accented mé of mé-is: dex and tris are the two preparatory syllables, receiving Ti and Do. Then mé receives La, and is closes upon Sol. Thus the cadence is Ti–Do–La–Sol, fitted to dex-tris mé-is. No additional hollow note is required by this two-syllable word.

blocks.title: The number, the letter, and the ending
blocks.text:
The eight ordinary psalm tones correspond to the eight modes of the antiphons. Their numbers may be written I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, or 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. A psalm tone is a formula by which verses of unequal length may be sung: the words are recited upon the tenor, and the appointed syllables receive the cadences. The lesson “Chanting psalms” explains these parts of the verse.

In a designation such as 8G, the number 8 names the eighth tone, and G names its termination, or final cadence. Read 1A3 as the first tone with ending a³, printed “1. a³” in the Liber Usualis. The 3 distinguishes this ending from a and a²; it does not signify three accents, three repetitions, or the third mode.

The letters distinguish the endings within a tone. They refer to their concluding pitches, though an ornamented variant may rise from the note named: the eighth tone’s G* is such a case. The printed distinction between capitals and small letters, and any numeral or star attached to them, should therefore be retained when consulting the book. These are names of formulas, not modern key signatures. Their notes may be transposed together to suit the singers.

blocks.title: The ending is determined by the antiphon
blocks.text:
Several endings may belong to one tone, so that the close of the psalm may lead suitably to the return of its antiphon. The Liber Usualis directs that the final cadence be chosen according to the antiphon. The singer therefore follows the designation and notation supplied with it; an ending is not chosen merely because its last note is familiar.

For the ordinary first tone, the tenor is La (A), and the mediation has two accents. For the ordinary eighth tone, the tenor is Do (C), and the mediation has one accent. Both endings studied here have one accent with two preparatory syllables. These particulars belong to the specified formulas; other tones have other arrangements.

blocks.title: 1A3: the first tone, ending a³
blocks.text:
With the same clef, the first tone begins Di = Fa and xit = Sol–La. The two rising notes on xit belong to that one syllable. The reciting note is La. At the mediation the accented Dó of Dómino receives Ti-flat, mi and no receive La, mé receives Sol, and o returns to La. The flat lowers Ti only; it does not lower the whole phrase.

In the second half, Sé-de a is recited upon La. The preparation gives dex = Sol and tris = Fa. In ending a³ the accented mé receives Sol–La, and the final is likewise receives Sol–La. Each pair is a podatus: sing its lower note before its upper note, keeping both notes upon the same syllable. The verse therefore ends upon La, although the first mode has Re for its modal final. The final of the mode and the last note of every psalm termination must not be confused.

blocks.title: Why a, a², and a³ are distinct
blocks.text:
These three terminations belong to the same first tone and share the preparation Sol–Fa. On the words mé-is, ending a gives Sol to mé and La to is; ending a² gives Sol to mé and Sol–La to is; ending a³ gives Sol–La to both syllables. All three reach La, but their approaches differ. The numeral is therefore needed to identify the melody.

The comparison retains Sé-de a déx-tris before each ending, so that the departure from the tenor may be heard. Its application is that of the two-syllable word mé-is. When another text requires an additional syllable, consult the hollow note in the formula and the worked verse, as explained in “Chanting psalms.”

blocks.title: The vowels E u o u a e
blocks.text:
At the close of an antiphon, the vowels E u o u a e may be placed beneath the notes of the psalm ending. They stand for the six syllables of sæ-cu-ló-rum A-men, the conclusion of the Gloria Patri. They indicate the termination to be used with the psalm; they are not an additional word of the antiphon.

The examples supply the complete syllables in place of these vowels. In 8G they receive Do, Do, Ti, Do, La, Sol. In 1. a³ they receive La, La, Sol, Fa, Sol–La, Sol–La. Here lo and rum prepare the accented A of Amen. The same formula is adapted throughout the psalm to the words of each verse; it does not allot six syllables to every verse ending.

blocks.title: Preparing a psalm from its designation
blocks.text:
First read the tone number and its complete ending designation. Observe the clef, find the tenor, and distinguish the mediation from the termination. Read the Latin before singing; then locate the cadence accents and count back the preparatory syllables. Where a hollow note occurs, use it only as required by the text and the worked formula.

Sing the first verse with its intonation; in ordinary psalmody begin the succeeding verses directly upon the tenor. The prescribed repetition of the intonation in certain canticles is a separate rule. When the psalm is concluded, return to the antiphon as directed. The examples in this lesson are educational adaptations of the printed formulas and verses; the instrumental sound illustrates their pitches and timing, while the syllables show how the voice is to carry the words.

blocks.title: The preparation of the text
blocks.text:
Before the melody is attempted, the text should be understood as fully as possible and distinctly pronounced. The source follows Roman ecclesiastical usage. The accent gives life to the word by a light upward impulse; the weaker syllables must nevertheless receive their full articulation. Thus Dó-mi-ne and déx-te-ra retain their middle syllables. Prolongation in the melody does not confer the word accent upon an unaccented syllable.

The English comparisons which follow are approximate aids to pronunciation. The vowels should remain pure, without the gliding sounds common in English. As the Cantor Guide provides no spoken Latin, the written divisions serve for preparation of the words, and the instrumental examples for study of the melody.

blocks.title: Pure vowels
blocks.text: A · E · I · O · U · Y
blocks.detail: A is open, as in “father”; E resembles the vowel of “red,” without the glide heard in “ray”; I is sounded as “ee” in “feet”; O is pure and rounded, approximated by “for” without the R; U is sounded as “oo” in “moon.” Y has the sound of I. The quality of these vowels must remain unaltered before M, N, or R.

blocks.title: Separate vowels and diphthongs
blocks.text: Dí-e-i · fí-li-i · cáe-lum · láu-da
blocks.detail: Adjacent vowels ordinarily form separate syllables, as in di-e-i, fi-li-i, e-o-rum, and a-it. AE and OE have the single sound of E. In AU, EU, and AY, the two vowels belong to one syllable: the first is sustained throughout the melisma, and the second introduced at the passage to the following syllable. EI is ordinarily divided, as in me-i, with the exception of the interjection hei.

blocks.title: QU, GU, and cui
blocks.text: Qui · sánguis · cú-i
blocks.detail: U following Q, or NG before a vowel as in sanguis, is united with the following vowel in one syllable, while retaining its own sound. Cui ordinarily has two syllables, cu-i; in hymns, however, the source observes that the metre may require one.

blocks.title: C, CC, SC, and CH
blocks.text: Cáe-lum · éc-ce · de-scén-dit
blocks.detail: Before E, AE, OE, I, or Y, C is sounded as “ch” in “church,” CC as the joined sound “t-ch,” and SC as “sh.” In other positions C has the sound of K. CH is always sounded as K, even before E or I. Thus the initial sound of caelum is ch, that of caritas is k, and machina also has the sound k.

blocks.title: G and GN
blocks.text: Re-gí-na · Má-gni-fi-cat
blocks.detail: Before E, AE, OE, I, or Y, G is soft, as in “generous”; elsewhere it is hard, as in “go.” GN forms a single joined sound, as in Italian, approximated by ny. Thus Magnificat may be represented approximately as mah-nyee-fee-caht. A separate hard g must not precede the n.

blocks.title: H, J, and R
blocks.text: Ní-hil · mí-hi · al-le-lú-ia
blocks.detail: H is ordinarily silent. In nihil, mihi, and their compounds, the source assigns it the sound of K. J, frequently written I, has the sound of Y and is joined to the following vowel. R should be lightly rolled, without altering the preceding vowel to the English R-coloured sound; the ee vowels of Ky-ri-e must remain pure.

blocks.title: TI and TH
blocks.text: Grá-ti-a · pa-ti-én-ti-a
blocks.detail: TI before another vowel is pronounced tsee, except after S, X, or T. In other cases T retains its ordinary sound. TH is pronounced simply T, as in Thomas and catholicam. Each written syllable of patientia is to be distinctly articulated, without contraction to an English equivalent.

blocks.title: S, X, XC, and Z
blocks.text: Mi-se-ri-cór-di-a · ex-cél-sis
blocks.detail: In the source’s account, S is ordinarily unvoiced, with a slight softening between vowels. X is sounded as ks, likewise softened between vowels. XC before E, AE, OE, I, or Y is pronounced ksh, as in excelsis; elsewhere the hard sequence k-s-k is retained. Z has the sound dz. The remaining consonants receive their familiar sounds and should be distinctly articulated.

blocks.title: Double consonants
blocks.text: Bel-lo · Ab-bas · ter-ra
blocks.detail: Both consonants must be distinctly sounded: bel-lo differs from the English “bellow.” The first closes the preceding syllable, and the second opens that which follows. Their articulation must neither introduce another vowel nor interrupt the musical phrase.

blocks.title: Word accent and sentence shape
blocks.text: Pá-ter nós-ter · Dó-mi-nus
blocks.detail: The accented syllable receives a light upward impulse, after which the word passes towards repose. The weak middle syllable of Dó-mi-nus must retain its full articulation. In the sentence, related words are united and the principal word receives its due prominence. The meaning of the phrase should therefore be considered before its breathing is determined.

blocks.title: Unity in singing
blocks.text:
Each singer should attend to the others, that the voices may unite in a common sound. Pitch, movement, entries, and breathing should be agreed upon beforehand. Clear pronunciation, even movement, and a common understanding of the phrase secure this unity more surely than exaggerated effects. Both undue haste and laborious dragging are to be avoided.

A passage may first be studied slowly in the Cantor Guide, and afterwards resumed at a flowing pace. The organ, harp, and tone sounds are aids to practice. The delicate release of a phrase, the light passage of a liquescent note, and the inflection of the Latin accent remain the work of the singing voice.

blocks.title: The source’s directions for the Mass
blocks.text:
The directions on pages xv–xvj concern the Mass. They assign the intonations to the cantors or celebrant, regulate the alternation of the Kyrie and other chants, and indicate by asterisks the entry of the choir. The Gradual, Alleluia, Tract, and sequences are treated with their seasonal distinctions.

Further directions concern the addition of psalm verses to processional antiphons, suitable Latin singing at the Offertory and Communion, and the prescribed silence during the Consecration. Responses at the conclusion of Mass are specified, together with provision for recitation upon one note or a psalm tone when the appointed chant cannot practicably be sung. This account records the Mass directions of the volume; their scope does not extend to the 1960 Divine Office provided in Hours.

blocks.title: About this adaptation
blocks.text:
This guide is adapted from The Liber Usualis, with Introduction and Rubrics in English, edited by the Benedictines of Solesmes, Desclée & Co., 1961, printed pages xj–xxxix, with the psalm-tone tables on Arabic pages 112–117 and worked verses on pages 128 and 133. The instruction has been abridged and arranged in lessons, with care to retain the manner of the source. It is an educational adaptation; its wording is not a verbatim transcription. References follow the printed pagination; Arabic page references are distinguished from those to the Roman-numbered introduction.

The volume contains both the Vatican preface and the later Solesmes Rules for Interpretation. Where their accounts differ, the distinction is retained and the practical teaching of the latter is followed. This applies particularly to the quilisma, the rhythmic ictus, repeated notes, and certain alternatives in psalm cadences. The teaching is therefore that of a particular historical school, without claiming to exhaust the interpretation of chant.

blocks.title: About the examples
blocks.text:
Examples marked “Teaching” have been composed for illustration. Those marked “Adapted” retain musical or verbal patterns from the source in a simplified form. The general formulas and explanatory brackets indicate relationships; they add no notes to be sung. The psalm examples explain the reading of a formula; the chant and cadence for prayer are supplied in the Office itself.

The source’s comparisons with five-line notation are here explained by square notation and solfège. The PDF and its page images are not included in Hours. A glossary is available from the contents menu, with references to the corresponding lessons.

glossary.definition: A chant associated with a psalm; its melody helps determine the psalm’s final cadence.
The rising movement and repose of rhythm, according to the Solesmes teaching of the source.
The melodic formula that closes a half-verse or verse.
A sign naming the note on its line: Do for the C clef, Fa for the F clef. Its position determines the names of all the other lines and spaces.
A guide to the next staff’s first pitch; it is not an extra note.

glossary.term: E u o u a e
glossary.definition: The vowels of sæculorum Amen, placed beneath the notes to indicate the psalm termination associated with an antiphon.
A rhythmic mark: horizontal for broadening, vertical for a rhythmic step, with the source’s special salicus qualification.
A downward bend subdividing a long first half of a psalm verse.
The rhythmic step or point of alighting; it does not of itself require an accent or greater intensity.
An opening formula that establishes the chant and leads to the choir’s entry or psalm tenor.
A light vocal transition associated with a diphthong or consonant combination.
The psalm cadence at the middle asterisk.
Several notes sung on one syllable.
A melodic organization involving a resting note, range, and characteristic intervals.
A dot that doubles the preceding note in the source’s practical method.
A written sign or group of notes forming a melodic movement upon a syllable.
A special note form whose interpretation depends on its relationship to the surrounding group.
Adjacent groups meeting on the same pitch, with the joined notes sustained together.
A formula of intonation, recitation, and cadences by which the verses of a psalm are sung.
A jagged note approached with lengthening of the preceding note in the Solesmes method.
An ascending group with a specially supported and lengthened note in this source’s interpretation.
The names Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti used to follow scale relationships.
The reciting note of a psalm tone.
The final cadence of a psalm tone, determined by the antiphon; a letter and, where needed, a numeral or star distinguish its form.
A psalm-tone family with a change of reciting note between the halves.
